content: News Data Institute Science Healthcare Genomics: Predicting disease risk and outcomes to guide care News Article by the Communications Team 25 Nov 2026 The Wellcome Sanger Institute has renamed its Human Genetics programme to Healthcare Genomics. Email newsletter News and blog updates Sign up Healthcare Genomics will use genetic data, longitudinal molecular measurements and clinical information to develop models that predict who is likely to develop disease, how it will progress and how patients might respond to treatment. Working closely with healthcare partners, Sanger Institute researchers will evaluate whether using these predictions to inform clinical decisions can improve patient care. Over the last twenty years, large-scale genetic studies have transformed our understanding of human disease, identifying thousands of genetic associations and providing important insights into disease biology. However, these advances have not yet given us the ability to reliably predict how disease will progress in individual patients. People with the same diagnosis can experience very different outcomes. One may respond well to treatment and remain relatively well, while another could develop serious complications or fail to respond to successive treatments. Healthcare Genomics, led by Dr Carl Anderson, aims to generate molecular data from hundreds of thousands of patient samples collected during routine healthcare, including repeat samples from the same patients, and combine these data with genetic information and linked clinical records. By measuring how patients’ biology changes throughout disease and treatment, researchers will use advanced statistical and computational approaches, including artificial intelligence (AI), to build models that predict disease progression, treatment response and other important clinical outcomes. Alongside this, genetic data will help identify the biological mechanisms driving disease and potential targets for new treatments. “Our ambition is to give clinicians the tools to predict how a patient’s disease is likely to progress, whether they are at risk of serious complications, and which treatments and interventions are most likely to benefit them. Making these predictions reliably for individual patients is one of the greatest challenges in medicine. Meeting that challenge will require us to bring together genetics, longitudinal molecular data, clinical information and new computational approaches at scale. I’m hugely excited about the opportunity to tackle these challenges with colleagues and partners, and to undertake research that could make a profound difference to the lives of so many patients.” Dr Carl Anderson , Head of Healthcare Genomics at the Wellcome Sanger Institute Healthcare Genomics will build on the Sanger Institute’s strengths in human genetics, large-scale data generation and analysis, and open science. The Institute will expand the programme’s faculty, recruiting researchers with expertise in areas such as AI and real-world clinical data analysis to complement its existing scientific strengths. Working closely with partners across healthcare, academia and industry in the UK and internationally, the programme will develop and test predictive models on anonymised data from people of different ancestries and in different healthcare settings, establishing how reliably the models perform across diverse populations and contexts. Crucially, the programme will go beyond developing predictive models to evaluate whether using them to guide clinical decisions can improve patient outcomes and make more effective use of healthcare resources. The predictive models developed by Healthcare Genomics could contribute towards a learning healthcare system, in which tools developed through research are tested and applied in routine clinical care. As new molecular measurements and clinical information are collected through ongoing patient care, these data can be used to evaluate, refine and improve the models, creating a continuous cycle of research, clinical application and improvement. “At the Wellcome Sanger Institute we are investing in new expertise and strengthening partnerships across healthcare, academia and industry to bring together the capabilities needed to deliver this ambitious scientific programme. Predictive medicine has enormous potential to improve healthcare, but realising that potential will require sustained investment, long-term collaboration and a commitment to demonstrating clinical benefit. The Healthcare Genomics programme is committed to playing its part in making that happen, with a strong open science ethos at its core.” Professor Matt Hurles , Director at the Wellcome Sanger Institute More information Related blog posts 20 Nov 2026 “You never know how your life is going to end up.” – Gosia Trynka on immune genomics, the beauty of hindsight and the strong women who shaped her Gosia Trynka is a Group Leader at the Wellcome Sanger Institute and Science Direct
